reports.name: Jacob Misiorowski
reports.published_report: A 37.9% strikeout rate with a 2.13 xERA is a rare combination — most guys who miss bats this relentlessly give some of it back with the walk rate, but Misiorowski's 6.6% BB% sits comfortably below where you'd expect the control tax to land. The 100.6 mph fastball with 2635 rpm spin explains why hitters are whiffing at 37.3% of pitches, and a 3.6% barrel rate tells you the contact they do make isn't doing much damage. The projection calls for 247 strikeouts over 183.3 innings with a 2.938 ERA, which would actually be conservative relative to what the Statcast profile says he already is. The one dependency worth naming: if the command slips and that BB% climbs into the double digits, the whole thing gets more volatile fast.

reports.name: James Wood
reports.published_report: The xwOBA is .403 and the barrel rate is 18.6%, both at the 99th and 100th percentile respectively — the contact quality is about as loud as it gets. The wrinkle is a 28.7% strikeout rate that sits in the bottom tenth of the league, which is what happens when elite chase avoidance (21.3%, 94th percentile) coexists with a 30.1% whiff rate on pitches he does swing at: he's disciplined enough to draw walks at a 16.4% clip, but pitchers have learned to attack him in the zone and make him miss. If he tightens the swing-and-miss without sacrificing the approach, the .887 OPS projection is probably a floor; if the strikeout rate climbs further, the .267/.380/.507 line is what you get, which is still a productive everyday corner outfielder with 34-homer upside.

reports.name: Pete Crow-Armstrong
reports.published_report: The xSLG sits at .508 (97th percentile) while the xBA is .264 (75th percentile), which tells you exactly what kind of hitter this is: someone who hits the ball very hard when he makes contact, but chases enough, 34.2% (23rd percentile), that the contact comes with a tax. The 11.4% walk rate softens that somewhat, keeping the xwOBA at .374, and 29.5 ft/s sprint speed opens up a 33-homer, 34-steal projection that very few players can credibly threaten. The whole profile hinges on whether the chase rate stays manageable enough to keep pitchers from burying him, because if it climbs, the strikeout rate (already 25.8%) follows, and that elite slugging gets rationed by a shrinking number of decent pitches to handle.

reports.name: Bobby Witt Jr.

His xwOBA (.378) and xSLG (.504) are built on 92.2 mph average exit velocity and a 50.3% hard-hit rate, a contact shape that earns every bit of the underlying numbers. reports.name: Kevin McGonigle
reports.published_report: The discipline profile here is legitimately rare: a 19.6% chase rate sitting at the 98th percentile, paired with a 13.4% walk rate and a 14.1% strikeout rate that together sketch a hitter who almost never gives away an at-bat. The .355 xwOBA earns its 88th-percentile slot not through brute force, because the 87.8 mph average exit velocity and 37.6% hard-hit rate both run well below average, but through the sheer volume of quality contact his plate discipline manufactures. That translates to a .277/.373/.454 line with 21 home runs across 662 projected plate appearances, power output that depends entirely on his continuing to work counts into hittable pitches rather than on any latent raw strength. If the contact quality stagnates where it sits now, he's a .280 on-base machine who tops out as a second-division regular at third; if the discipline holds and the exit velocity ticks even modestly, he profiles as a genuine everyday piece.

reports.name: Paul Skenes

reports.name: Cam Schlittler
reports.published_report: The xERA sits at 2.85 and the strikeout rate is 31.4%, yet the contact-quality numbers are almost aggressively ordinary — barrel rate at 7.3%, hard-hit at 38.3%, both right around the middle of the league. That gap tells you exactly what he is: a pitcher who wins by getting to two strikes and making hitters swing at pitches they can't barrel, not by inducing weak contact once the ball is in play. The 98.0 mph fastball with 2540 rpm spin is the engine for a 34.4% chase rate, and when hitters do make contact, they aren't doing much damage mostly because they're late or off-balance rather than getting robbed by soft stuff. If the chase rate regresses toward league norms, the ERA climbs toward the 3.319 ValuCast projects over 192.9 innings, and the whole profile thins considerably.

reports.name: Logan Gilbert
reports.published_report: The Statcast profile here has a seam worth pulling on: elite contact-avoidance sitting alongside contact-quality numbers that look like a liability. Gilbert's 30.7% whiff rate and 6.5% walk rate are both well above average, the kind of combination that keeps innings clean and pitch counts manageable across a full rotation season. If his whiff rate softens at all, the contact-quality floor is exposed and the ERA climbs in a hurry.

reports.name: Taj Bradley
reports.published_report: The strikeout rate and the contact quality are pulling in exactly opposite directions, and that tension is the whole profile. Bradley's 27.4% K% sits in a genuinely good place, and his 97.2 mph fastball explains how he gets there, but hitters are barreling him at 9.1% with a 45.4% hard-hit rate, both near the bottom of the league. He misses bats at a solid 27.4% whiff rate while generating almost no chase at 28.3%, which means the swings he earns tend to come in the zone, and in-zone contact against that kind of velocity can still be loud. The 10.2% walk rate is the quiet killer: it keeps the bases populated enough that the hard contact matters more, and a 4.022 ERA projection with a 1.296 WHIP is what you get when elite stuff and poor command share a uniform.

reports.name: Jacob Young
reports.published_report: The legs are the profile. At 29.1 ft/s sprint speed, Young is genuinely elite on the bases, and the 18 projected steals in the projection understates how much that speed shapes his value. The contact reads are the honest surprise: a 16.6% strikeout rate and a 20.8% whiff rate say he actually makes consistent contact, but the exit velocity profile, 87.7 mph average with a 31.4% hard-hit rate, tells you the bat isn't doing damage when it connects. That gap between a respectable xBA of .257 and a soft xSLG of .383 is the whole tension in this profile: he's a guy who puts ball in play without the power to punish mistakes, and whether the .707 OPS projection means anything depends almost entirely on whether the 7.0% walk rate climbs enough to leverage the speed into on-base value. A low-end regular if the game keeps giving him green lights; a bench outfielder with a loud tool if it doesn't.

reports.name: José Soriano
reports.published_report: The gap between a 28.6% whiff rate and a 4.45 xERA is the whole Soriano puzzle, and the walk rate is what creates it. Hitters chase at 32.8% and miss at a clip well above league average, yet his 9.8 BB% bleeds away whatever trouble those swings cause, and the .323 xwOBA lands in a genuinely concerning place. The 97.1 mph fastball is loud enough to explain the whiff and chase numbers, but the spin on it sits at the 5th percentile, which means the ride hitters expect from that velocity isn't there, and when they do make contact they're squaring it up at a rate that keeps the xERA fat. The projection's 3.797 ERA over 184.2 innings is essentially a bet that sequencing and defense bail him out of a Statcast profile that hasn't earned it yet, and the read here is that he profiles as a back-end starter whose ceiling is exactly that if the walks ever tighten, and a bullpen arm if they don't.

reports.name: Logan Henderson
reports.published_report: The xERA sits at 2.74 and the walk rate at 5.1%, and together they tell you almost everything about what Logan Henderson actually is right now. He's not blowing people away, with a fastball at 93.1 mph and a whiff rate that lands around the middle of the league, but the contact he does allow is soft enough and the walks rare enough that the underlying profile looks like a genuine mid-rotation arm who outperforms his stuff. Harrison's 27.9 K% sits in a strong percentile tier, and his 32.4% chase rate shows he's genuinely disrupting swings outside the zone, but when contact does land, it lands hard enough that his xERA settles at 4.01, right at the median for pitchers. The stuff earns the swing-and-miss; the barrel and exit velocity numbers say he hasn't found a consistent way to make contact weak. If the 2369 rpm spin on his fastball keeps generating deception up in the zone, he profiles as a durable mid-rotation arm who takes the ball every fifth day at a rate just above league average — if contact quality regresses toward him, the walks at 7.1% become the second problem instead of the third.

reports.name: Brandon Pfaadt
reports.published_report: The xERA sits at 3.92, but 133 projected strikeouts across 172.0 innings tells you everything about how he has to earn it. Pfaadt's 16.7% K% ranks in the 10th percentile among pitchers, so he lives and dies by limiting damage rather than missing bats, and that 5.7% BB% at the 91st percentile is what keeps the whole thing viable. The 2505 rpm fastball spin helps him suppress barrels, and the .305 xwOBA says genuine contact management is happening, but a 21.3% Whiff% leaves almost no margin when his command wavers. If the walk rate holds, he's a back-of-rotation contributor with a real floor; if it slips, there's not enough swing-and-miss to compensate, and that 4.532 ERA projection starts to look optimistic.

reports.name: Leo Bernal
reports.published_report: The translation is what makes this profile interesting: 20 K% and a 12 BB% at AAA become essentially league-average strikeout rates and above-average walk rates at the MLB level, which for a catcher at 22 is a real foundation. The .278/.363/.468 line at AAA across 432 plate appearances carries a .19 ISO, and while the MLB-equivalent power translates to a .151 ISO sitting right beside the 8.5% average walk rate context that makes the discipline look even better, the contact holds up more durably than the power does. If the bat-to-ball stays intact behind the dish, he's a functional everyday catcher; if the contact rate softens against better velocity, the whole thing collapses toward a backup with a useful eye.

reports.name: Kaelen Culpepper
reports.published_report: The profile that keeps pulling you back is the contact-power-speed combination at a position that rarely offers all three. At AAA in 2026, Culpepper is hitting .271/.367/.478 across 343 plate appearances, with 14 home runs and 17 stolen bases, while striking out just 18% of the time. The translation tightens things up some — ISO drops to .16 at the MLB level, strikeouts tick up to 20.7%, but the walk rate translates to 9.8% against a MLB average that sits at 8.5%, and the contact profile holds enough shape to believe the hit tool carries. The ceiling here is a bench or platoon bat at short, which is genuinely useful, and the floor is organizational depth; what determines which end he lands on is whether the power holds even slightly against big-league arms, because the .16 ISO equivalent doesn't leave much margin.

reports.name: Michael McGreevy
reports.published_report: The Statcast profile is almost uniformly bottom-decile: a 16.4% strikeout rate, a 20.1% whiff rate, and an xERA of 5.37 that sits at the 8th percentile. The one real asset is a 6.8% walk rate that grades well above average, which is the only thing keeping this profile from being a pure liability. Everything here hinges on contact management, and right now hitters are barreling him at a 9.1% clip with a 41.8% hard-hit rate — the contact he does allow is loud. A 4.29 ERA projection over 150.4 innings is generous relative to what the underlying numbers say, and if the gap between ERA and xERA doesn't close, he's a back-end arm fighting for a rotation spot rather than holding one.

reports.name: Kash Mayfield
reports.published_report: The 19% K-BB% tells you what kind of pitcher he is before anything else does: not a swing-and-miss guy, a command guy. Kash Mayfield has struck out 62 batters across 53.3 innings at A+ with a 1.2 WHIP, and the shape of it, 90th-percentile WHIP, 83rd-percentile K-BB%, 71st-percentile walk rate, says the control is doing the heavy lifting where the pure stuff isn't. The translation is honest about the ceiling: at MLB-equivalent rates, his K/9 sits just below league average and his walk rate runs a tick above it, which puts the floor squarely in depth arm territory if the command advantage compresses under better hitters. If it holds, the lane is multi-inning reliever or setup piece, two to three years out.

reports.name: Emerson Hancock
reports.published_report: The walk rate is the whole argument here. At 5.7%, Hancock sits in the 91st percentile for BB%, and that number is doing a lot of heavy lifting for a pitcher whose strikeout rate (22.3%) and chase rate (28.5%) are both below the median. He throws strikes, hitters make contact, and that contact is hard, 41.6% hard-hit rate and an average exit velocity of 89.7 mph that ranks near the bottom of the league. The xERA of 4.01 and the projection of 4.124 ERA over 159.1 innings say the same thing: a back-of-the-rotation starter who stays in games not because he misses bats but because he doesn't beat himself. If the zone command slips, there isn't a strikeout rate to catch him.

Ninety-four walks in 640 AAA plate appearances in 2026, a 15% clip that translates to 12.3% at the MLB level while the MLB average sits at 8.5%, and suddenly the .400 OBP stops looking like an inflated Triple-A number. The 20 home runs and .18 ISO at AAA get humbled by the translation, landing at .146 MLB-equivalent right at the MLB average of .150, so the ceiling is narrowly drawn: the approach and the legs, 28 stolen bases at AAA, are carrying this profile more than the power is. If that patience holds against better velocity and tighter zones, Ehrhard is either a genuine bench bat with real on-base value or, if pitchers find the edges he can't handle, 129 strikeouts in a full season is the lever that turns a functional profile into a fringe one.

reports.name: Matthew Liberatore
reports.published_report: The Statcast profile is a problem. A 5.02 xERA and a .341 xwOBA both sit at the 13th percentile, and the contact quality numbers back them up: a 9.3% barrel rate and 42.4% hard-hit rate both near the bottom of the league. His strikeout and walk rates land right at the median, which means he's not missing enough bats to compensate for the damage when hitters do connect. The projection absorbs some of that, landing at a 4.207 ERA over 131.1 innings, but that gap between xERA and projected ERA is the whole argument — it requires the soft-contact luck or sequencing to run considerably better than what the batted-ball profile suggests it should. If the contact quality stays where it is, what's left is a backend arm running out of rope every fifth day.

reports.name: Cam Cauley
reports.published_report: The stolen base number is the loudest thing in this profile, and it's worth sitting with: 39 steals across 434 AAA plate appearances in 2026, paired with a .366 OBP that translates to a 10.4% walk rate at the MLB level. The bat plays as a genuine complement to the speed, .276/.366/.470 at AAA with 16 home runs and an ISO that translates to .154 at the MLB level, right at the league average threshold for power, so this isn't a slap-hitter living on legs alone. The ceiling is a bench or platoon bat, not a regular, and the profile hinges on whether that contact quality holds against better stuff, because the MLB-equivalent K rate sits at 21.9%, essentially league average, leaving no margin for erosion. If the plate discipline holds and the speed stays, he's a useful piece; if the hit tool erodes, the stolen bases become a footnote.

reports.name: Kyle Tucker
reports.published_report: The walk rate tells most of the story: 12.4% BB with a 16.7% K rate is a genuinely rare contact-and-discipline combination, and that's what props up a .331 xwOBA even as the raw power metrics sit well below average. His 6.4% barrel rate and 88.5 mph average exit velocity aren't the engine here. Plate discipline is, and when a hitter earns that many free passes while barely striking out, the .356 OBP projection earns its credibility without needing elite thump behind it. The risk is tightly bound to that discipline holding: if pitchers find a consistent way to attack him given the sprint speed (26.7 ft/s) and modest hard-hit numbers, there isn't a carrying tool waiting in reserve. Keep him as a corner outfielder who gets on base at a rate most middle-of-the-order hitters don't, projecting to a .799 OPS, and that's the floor and ceiling, reasonably close together.

reports.name: Daniel Eagen
reports.published_report: The strikeout-to-walk profile is the argument: 157 strikeouts against 41 walks across 122 AA innings, a K-BB% that ranks 94th percentile among qualified pitchers and translates to 15.5% at the MLB level, where the average sits around 13.5%. That shape holds up at 11.6 K/9 and 3.0 BB/9 in the actual environment, and the ERA sitting at 4.7 with a 1.20 WHIP suggests the contact outcomes are lagging the command profile, not leading it. If the stuff translates into a big-league strike zone the way the peripherals suggest it might, Eagen becomes a reliable multi-inning or setup arm within a year or two; if the contact damage follows him up a level, the floor is depth.

reports.name: Brady Ebel
reports.published_report: The walk rate is the whole profile. Across A+ & A in 538 plate appearances, Brady Ebel drew 105 walks against 114 strikeouts, a 19% BB% that translates to 13.4% in MLB context — nearly five points clear of what the average big-leaguer posts. The power is where the read gets honest: a .154 ISO in the minors flattens to .108 in translation, well short of the MLB mean, and a shortstop who can't threaten over the fence needs the discipline to age into something a lineup actually fears. If the plate discipline holds and the raw power develops even modestly, he becomes a useful on-base piece who can stay at short; if the power gap doesn't close, you've got a bench bat who takes pitches.

Either a fringy everyday regular if the contact improves, or a bench bat whose walks keep him employed.

reports.name: José Ramírez
reports.published_report: The Statcast profile here is built around contact and discipline, not raw power, and that's the honest shape of what he is at 34. A 12.7% strikeout rate with an 11.0% walk rate means he puts the ball in play constantly and rarely gives away an at-bat, and the 15.3% whiff rate backs that up as genuinely elite contact skill. The exit velocity and barrel rate are soft, 88.6 mph average and 4.1% barrels, so the .796 OPS projection leans on the .343 OBP and 30 projected steals doing real work. The whole profile holds if the sprint speed stays near 28.0 ft/s; if that slips, the stolen base contribution fades and what remains is a solid-contact, low-power third baseman carrying a full workload at 586 projected plate appearances.

His xwOBA sits at .402 and his average exit velocity at 93.9 mph, both at the 98th or 99th percentile, so the gap between his actual production and what he deserves tends to close by year's end rather than open up. The one friction in the profile is contact quality: a 24.1% strikeout rate drags on his .267 projection average, and if pitchers keep exploiting his whiff tendencies, the BA softens before the power does. What he is, settled and plainly, is a middle-of-the-order masher who profiles as one of the most dangerous hitters in any given lineup.

reports.name: Blake Mitchell
reports.published_report: The walk rate is the loudest thing in this profile, and it's also where the argument gets complicated. At A+ this season, Mitchell drew 113 walks across 511 plate appearances, a 22% clip that grades at the 99th percentile against his peer pool, and it's dragging a .414 OBP out of a .234 average. The power translates cautiously, his A+ ISO of .226 melts to .152 at the MLB-equivalent level, sitting right at the MLB average of .150, and 174 strikeouts in that same 511-PA sample produce a translation of 36.8% against a catching corps that generally can't sustain contact that thin. Catching is a position where you can carry a loud strikeout rate if the walk rate stays elite and the power holds shape, but if that discipline erodes under better pitching, the .234 average doesn't leave much underneath it. A bench receiver at best, organizational depth at worst, and the catcher's position premium is the only thing keeping this profile interesting at all.

At AA in 2026, Drew Beam has posted a 6.9 K/9 with a 6.50 ERA across 129 innings, and when you translate that strikeout rate to an MLB context it comes in at 6.5 while the MLB average sits at 8.6 — a gap that leaves almost no margin for anything else to go wrong. The control is genuinely fine; his 2.9 BB/9 at AA translates to exactly league-average walk rate, which is a real skill, but a pitcher who misses bats at the 6th percentile of his peer pool needs control that does more than match the field. If the strikeout rate doesn't tick up meaningfully, what remains is a depth arm, and that's the ceiling the profile already names.

reports.name: Dylan Dreiling
reports.published_report: The .312 average and .896 OPS at AA are loud, and they should be — 538 plate appearances is a real season, not a hot week. What complicates the read is the translation: the power that looks like a carrying tool at AA (.204 ISO, 22 home runs) softens to a .154 MLB equivalent, and the strikeout rate ticks up to 23.1% against a game where the average hitter strikes out 22.0% of the time. The walk rate translates cleanly at 9.0%, but that's a support beam, not a foundation. If the power holds any of its AA shape in the upper levels, Dreiling is a useful left-handed center fielder who can spell an everyday player and take a walk; if the ISO just melts on contact with better arms, what's left is a high-BABIP profile that won't survive the jump.

reports.name: Trevor Megill
reports.published_report: A 38.6% chase rate puts him at the 99th percentile, and that single number explains most of what's going on here. Hitters are chasing his stuff out of the zone at an elite clip, which props up a 30.5% whiff rate and keeps the hard contact manageable even with an average exit velo sitting at 90.5 mph, a figure that looks alarming until you remember that exit velo on contact matters far less when you're rarely giving hitters pitches to square up in the first place. The xERA of 2.64 and xwOBA of .252 both sit at the 96th percentile, and a 3.531 ERA projection with 28 saves in 64 innings suggests some regression from that Statcast baseline, which is fair — the contact-quality numbers carry a real tension between the miss-rate story and the hard-hit rate when hitters do connect. Milwaukee's closer job is his if the chase rate holds.

If the strikeout rate doesn't bend at the highest level, the walks and the pop become decorative.

reports.published_report: The .444 OBP at A-ball is loud, but a .439 BABIP is doing most of the carrying. Gonzalez is 19, posting a 1.01 OPS across 153 plate appearances, with 21 walks against 30 strikeouts and 13 stolen bases, so the athletic and zone-feel indicators are both pointing the right direction for his age. reports.name: Brian Curley

The problem is everything else: a 5.3 ERA and 1.5 WHIP suggest the strike-throwers are getting hit, and 130 strikeouts across AA & A+ produce a K/9 that translates to 8.0 at the MLB level, a tick below average, leaving almost no margin for error when contact does happen. reports.name: Aroon Escobar
reports.published_report: The profile that stands out here isn't the bat — it's the discipline and the legs. Across 569 plate appearances at AA, Escobar has drawn 67 walks against 92 strikeouts, and that patience translates to a 9.9% walk rate at the MLB-equivalent level, a tick better than the 8.5% MLB average. Twenty-seven stolen bases give him a carrying tool the bat doesn't yet provide. The contact quality isn't hiding anything: a .230 average, .117 ISO, and .258 BABIP are exactly what they look like, and the MLB-equivalent ISO of .105 sits well short of the .150 MLB average. If the discipline and speed translate, he's a bench bat with genuine on-base utility; if the bat never develops even modest pop, the ceiling is organizational depth and not much else.

Jay Allen II is hitting .267/.363/.438 in 465 plate appearances, but the MLB-equivalent translation deflates each piece: strikeout rate climbs to 25.5%, walk rate slips to 8.2% when the MLB average sits at 8.5%, and ISO shrinks from .171 to .137. The speed survives that filter; the power and plate discipline don't quite make it through. If the hit tool holds and the legs stay legitimate against better competition, he's a fringy bench outfielder who can run; if the bat doesn't sharpen, there isn't enough else to carry a roster spot.

reports.name: Kyle DeBarge
reports.published_report: Forty-one stolen bases at AA is the loudest thing on this card, and it's carrying a profile that doesn't have much else going for it. The bat is a real problem: a .221/.325/.352 line in 533 plate appearances, and when the translation runs through the AA-to-MLB filter, the strikeout rate climbs to 27.7% while the ISO lands at .113, well below what a typical big-leaguer produces. The walk rate translates to 10.3%, a tick above the MLB mean of 8.5%, so the on-base instincts are there, but they're propping up a hit tool that grades in the bottom quarter of the pool and power that simply isn't going to play up a level. If the speed stays elite and the contact improves enough to make it actionable, there's a bench piece here, a late-inning pinch runner or defensive replacement who can steal a bag; if the strikeout rate holds at its current shape through the upper minors, that's organizational depth.

reports.name: Mitch Voit
reports.published_report: Forty-five stolen bases across AA & A+ is the loudest thing on this card, and it's sitting next to a profile that otherwise grades out as organizational depth. The contact and patience are real enough: .273/.372 with 51 walks against 94 strikeouts in 483 plate appearances, and the walk rate translates to an MLB equivalent of 8.8%, roughly in line with where the league sits. The power doesn't travel well — that .158 ISO across the two levels flattens to a .123 MLB equivalent, and without more thump the speed becomes a tool in search of a role rather than a separator. If the gap power develops, he's a speed-first utility shortstop with enough bat to stick; if it doesn't, the legs alone won't get him past a bench conversation.

reports.name: Sabin Ceballos
reports.published_report: The walk rate is the loudest thing in this profile, and it's also the thing that exposes the ceiling problem. Ceballos has drawn 72 walks at AA in 504 plate appearances, a 14% clip that translates to an 11.4% MLB-equivalent rate, well above the league norm of 8.5%, and his 18% strikeout rate at AA would play as roughly league average up top. The power, though, is the constraint: a .171 ISO at AA translates to .136 at the MLB level, below average, and at first base that gap matters more than anywhere else. The profile hinges entirely on whether the contact quality improves enough to make the plate discipline actionable, because a first baseman who posts an MLB-equivalent .136 ISO with a .227 average at AA isn't a regular regardless of how often he gets on base.

reports.name: Jared Serna
reports.published_report: The contact is the problem, and the rest of the profile knows it. Across 336 plate appearances at AAA, Serna is hitting .221 with a .235 BABIP, meaning the low average isn't bad luck — he's simply not making enough hard contact to sustain more. The 18% strikeout rate translates to a 20.1% clip against big-league pitching, which actually undercuts the MLB average of 22.0%, so the swing decisions aren't the disaster the batting line implies; 32 walks and 14 stolen bases give him real complementary tools. The translated ISO of .135 lands shy of where MLB hitters average out, and a second baseman without a hit tool and without plus raw power is asking a lot of the roster math to work out. Either something clicks with the bat and he's a useful bench piece, or the .235 BABIP is telling the whole truth and he tops out as organizational depth.
